stem: A pancreas islet waitlist candidate is placed on inactive status while temporarily unsuitable for transplant. According to OPTN Policy 3.6.A, how does waiting time accrue during inactivity?

options.text: Unlimited waiting time accrues while the candidate remains inactive
No waiting time accrues while the candidate remains inactive
Waiting time accrues only for the first 30 cumulative inactive days
Waiting time accrues only when listed for whole-organ pancreas transplantation

explanation.rationale_correct: OPTN Table 3-3 specifies that pancreas islet candidates accrue unlimited waiting time while inactive, similar to pancreas, kidney, and lung candidates.

rationale_incorrect.B: No inactive accrual applies to heart and liver candidates, not pancreas islet candidates.
rationale_incorrect.C: A 30-day cumulative inactive accrual limit applies to intestine candidates, not pancreas islet candidates.
rationale_incorrect.D: Pancreas islet inactive waiting-time rules apply to islet-listed candidates regardless of whole-organ listing.

primary_anchor.section: Policy 3.6.A → Table 3-3 Waiting Time for Inactive Candidates → Pancreas islet
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Pancreas islet … Unlimited time … Candidates accrue waiting time while inactive

references.locator: Policy 3.6.A → Table 3-3: Waiting Time for Inactive Candidates (pancreas islet candidates accrue unlimited waiting time while inactive); PDF p. 46 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Final OPTN Policy 3.6.A inactive-waiting-time organ entry; paired with pancreas unlimited (cctc-2077); anchor verified on optn-policies p. 46.

stem: When assessing deceased-donor infection risk before organ acceptance, which physical examination finding aligns with standard donor risk-assessment references?

options.text: Track marks suggesting recent drug use
Normal healing scars that automatically prohibit all donation
Absence of any donor chart or history review
Only recipient preference without donor examination

explanation.rationale_correct: Donor physical examination includes evidence of recent drug use such as track marks, along with signs of active infection, underlying disease, and other procurement abnormalities.

rationale_incorrect.B: Not every scar prohibits donation; specific infection and drug-use findings guide risk assessment.
rationale_incorrect.C: Physical examination supplements donor chart review rather than replacing all donor data review.
rationale_incorrect.D: Donor risk assessment requires structured evaluation rather than recipient preference alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Donor-Transmitted Infections → C. Physical Examination → 3.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Evidence of recent drug use such as track marks

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Donor-Transmitted Infections → C. Physical Examination → 3. (track marks suggesting recent drug use); PDF p. 181 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Donor physical-exam angle distinct from donor chart review (cctc-2076) and PHS consent (cctc-2023); anchor verified on Cupples p. 181.

stem: During pancreas transplant evaluation, a candidate with long-standing diabetes has documented pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. How should the coordinator classify this finding?

options.text: An indication category listed for pancreas transplant alone or pancreas after kidney transplantation
A finding that permanently excludes any pancreas transplantation
An indication relevant only to isolated kidney transplantation
A contraindication that prohibits all immunosuppression after transplant

explanation.rationale_correct: Pancreas transplant alone or pancreas after kidney transplantation is indicated for diagnosis of diabetes and for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency among eligible candidates.

rationale_incorrect.B: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency is listed among PTA/PAK indication categories rather than automatic exclusion.
rationale_incorrect.C: Exocrine insufficiency is a pancreas-transplant indication rather than an isolated kidney indication.
rationale_incorrect.D: Exocrine insufficiency relates to transplant candidacy assessment, not prohibition of all immunosuppression.

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 15 → Indications → A.2. (pancreatic exocrine insufficiency as PTA/PAK indication); PDF p. 825 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Pancreatic exocrine-insufficiency angle distinct from PTA metabolic criteria (cctc-1082) and PAK evaluation (cctc-2050); anchor verified on Cupples p. 825.

stem: When coordinating deceased-donor organ acceptance, which psychosocial history element is included in donor infection risk assessment per standard references?

options.text: Alcohol or drug abuse and incarceration history
Only the recipient's preferred hospital room color
Psychosocial history is never reviewed during donor assessment

explanation.rationale_correct: Donor risk assessment includes discussion of psychosocial history such as alcohol or drug abuse, incarceration, high-risk sexual behavior, tattoos, and body piercing.

rationale_incorrect.B: Donor risk assessment focuses on infection and behavioral exposures rather than recipient room preferences.
rationale_incorrect.C: Donor psychosocial history guides transmitted-infection risk rather than cosmetic medication choices.
rationale_incorrect.D: Psychosocial history is explicitly included in donor risk assessment.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Donor-Transmitted Infections → B. Donor Risk Assessment → 2.d.
